title: Lab 4 — Quiz 2
subtitle: Control of Growth — experiments and growth refresher

questions.prompt: In the spice vapor experiment, where is the cinnamon placed?

options.text: Spread on the inside of the lid, with the plate kept inverted
Sprinkled directly onto the agar surface
Mixed into the bacterial suspension first
Placed in a paper disc in the plate center

questions.explanation: 1 g of spice is spread on the inner surface of the lid; the inverted plate lets vapors rise to the agar.

why.B: Spice must never contact the agar — that ruins the experiment.
why.C: Spice goes in the lid so only vapors reach the agar.
why.D: Paper discs are used in the disinfectant experiment.

questions.prompt: In the UV experiment, why is half of each plate covered with a notecard?

options.text: To keep the agar from drying out under the lamp
To protect students' eyes from the UV light
The covered half is not exposed to UV, so it serves as a comparison
To hold the lid in place during exposure

questions.explanation: The covered side isn't exposed to UV; the uncovered side is. Comparing them shows UV's effect at each time point.

why.A: The card blocks UV so the two halves can be compared.
why.B: The card's purpose is the unexposed comparison half.
why.D: Lids are removed during UV exposure.

questions.prompt: What variable is tested across the four UV plates?

options.text: Distance of each plate from the UV lamp
Type of organism swabbed on each plate
Duration of UV exposure (30 s, 1 min, 5 min, 10 min)
Amount of cinnamon spread in each lid

questions.explanation: The question: how does duration of exposure influence UV's antimicrobial properties? Plates are exposed for 30 s, 1 min, 5 min and 10 min.

why.A: All plates sit in the chamber; exposure time is what changes.
why.B: Each table uses one organism for all plates.
why.D: Cinnamon is part of the spice experiment.

questions.prompt: Why is a 'Control' plate swabbed with the organism but given no treatment?

options.text: To confirm that the agar is sterile before use
To test whether UV light kills endospores
To show normal growth for comparison with the treated plates
To serve as a backup if another plate is dropped

questions.explanation: The untreated control shows how the organism grows without any treatment, so effects in the spice and UV plates can be judged.

why.A: A sterility check would be an uninoculated plate.
why.B: The control gets no treatment at all.
why.D: It's an experimental control, not a spare.

questions.prompt: How is each plate inoculated with the swab?

options.text: Drag across the whole surface, rotate 180°, and swab the whole surface again
Streak in four quadrants with stabs between them
Press the swab in the center and leave it there
Spread 50 µL with a sterile glass spreader

questions.explanation: Swab horizontally across the entire agar surface, rotate the plate 180°, swab again, then discard the swab in biohazard.

why.B: That's the quadrant streak plate method.
why.C: The entire surface must be covered for even growth.
why.D: That's the spread plate in the probiotic experiment.

questions.prompt: In the disinfectant experiment, how are the chemicals applied to the plate?

options.text: Chemicals are poured over the entire agar surface
Chemicals are placed in the lid like the spices
Paper discs soaked in each chemical are placed on the agar
The organism is mixed with each chemical in a tube

questions.explanation: Paper discs imbued with the selected chemicals (A–G) are placed on the agar surface.

why.A: Each chemical is on its own disc so they can be compared.
why.B: Spices are in the lid; disinfectants are on paper discs.
why.D: The plate is swabbed, then the discs are placed.

questions.prompt: In the skin degerming experiment, what serves as the comparison for each washed or wiped thumb?

options.text: An untreated thumb
A sterile plate with nothing added
A plate of pure E. coli
A thumb treated with bleach

questions.explanation: Picture the Plan: untreated left/right thumbs vs washed (soap) and wiped (alcohol) thumbs.

why.B: The comparison is the untreated thumb print.
why.C: No known organism is used as the comparison.
why.D: Bleach is a disinfectant, unsafe for skin.

questions.prompt: These red colonies are Serratia marcescens. At what temperature range is its red pigment, prodigiosin, produced?

options.text: 35°C to 40°C
20°C to 30°C
Above 45°C
Below 4°C

questions.explanation: S. marcescens (soil microbe, opportunistic pathogen) makes the red pigment prodigiosin only at lower temperatures (20–30°C).

why.A: Prodigiosin is temperature sensitive and made only at lower temperatures.
why.D: Refrigeration slows growth; pigment is made at 20–30°C.

questions.prompt: On this growth-rate graph, which group has the LOWEST optimum temperature?

options.text: Psychrophiles
Mesophiles
Thermophiles
Hyperthermophiles

questions.explanation: From coldest to hottest optimum: psychrophiles, mesophiles, thermophiles, hyperthermophiles.

why.B: Mesophiles grow best at moderate temperatures.
why.C: Thermophiles grow best at high temperatures.

questions.prompt: Why are the growth curves on this graph skewed toward the optimum temperature?

options.text: Cells divide faster when temperatures are too cold
Membranes freeze above the optimum temperature
Proteins denature rapidly once temperature rises past the optimum
Endospores form at the optimum temperature

questions.explanation: The skewing is thought to reflect rapid protein denaturation as temperature rises past the optimum.

why.B: Above optimum the issue is protein denaturation.

questions.prompt: On this bacterial growth curve, which phase shows NO increase in the number of living cells as the cells adjust?

options.text: Log phase
Lag phase
Stationary phase
Death phase

questions.explanation: Lag: no increase. Log: exponential increase. Stationary: plateau (division ≈ death). Death/decline: exponential decrease.

why.C: In stationary phase, division and death are roughly equal (a plateau).
why.D: Death phase is an exponential decrease.

questions.prompt: In the stationary phase of the growth curve:

options.text: Cells divide exponentially and numbers double each generation
Cell numbers decrease exponentially as cells die off
The rate of cell division and the rate of death are roughly equal
Cells are adjusting to the medium and not dividing yet

questions.explanation: Stationary phase is a plateau in the number of living cells.

questions.prompt: Bacterial population growth is based on which form of reproduction?

options.text: Budding
Binary fission
Spore formation
Meiosis

questions.explanation: Binary fission: DNA is replicated as the cell elongates, a septum forms, and two similar daughter cells separate.

why.A: Budding is another, less common type of bacterial reproduction.
why.C: Fungi reproduce by spores; bacterial endospores are for survival.

questions.prompt: An organism that does NOT use oxygen and CANNOT detoxify it is a(n):

options.text: Aerotolerant anaerobe
Microaerophile
Facultative anaerobe
Obligate anaerobe

questions.explanation: Obligate anaerobes neither use nor detoxify oxygen, so they grow only at the bottom of thioglycolate broth.

why.A: Aerotolerant anaerobes don't use O2 but can detoxify it.
why.B: Microaerophiles use O2 and detoxify it.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the oxygen groups is FALSE?

options.text: Aerotolerant anaerobes use oxygen for growth
Obligate aerobes use oxygen and detoxify it
Microaerophiles use oxygen and detoxify it
Obligate anaerobes neither use nor detoxify oxygen
Facultative anaerobes can detoxify oxygen

questions.explanation: Aerotolerant anaerobes do NOT use oxygen, but they can detoxify it (group 3).
